chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar from Imran ibn Musa from Musa ibn Ja'far from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal from Ibn Bukayr from Abd al-A'la, the freedman of the family of Sam, regarding the man who intends to travel in the month of Ramadan.
He said: 'He breaks the fast, even if he departs before the sun sets by a little.'
The first interpretation of what is in it is that it is a suspended report (mauqoof), not traced back (musnad) to any of the Imams (peace be upon them).
And whatever this ruling is, it is not contradicted by the numerous traced-back reports.

And if it were sound, the correct view regarding it is what we mentioned: that whoever departs before the sunset of the sun and had intended the journey the night before, it is permissible for him to break the fast.
Even though he thereby leaves a merit and neglects what is more preferable, but he is not thereby a sinner deserving punishment.

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And whoever is obliged to shorten (the prayer), it is not permissible for him to break the fast and shorten until the call to prayer of his country disappears from him (i.e., sunset).

key_terms.أَذَانُ مِصْرِهِ: Call to prayer of his country/place
key_terms.مَوْقُوفٌ: Suspended report (narration from a companion or tabi'i, not directly from an Imam)
key_terms.مُسْنَدٌ: Traced back directly to an Imam

ai.seo_question: Can a traveler break their Ramadan fast if they depart before sunset?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies the distinction between breaking the fast (iftar) and shortening prayers (qasr) for travelers, noting that while breaking the fast is permissible if the intention was made the night before, the ruling for shortening prayers requires waiting until sunset in the place of residence. This highlights the Shia juristic view that the traveler's status is determined by the time of departure relative to the sunset call to prayer, ensuring the fast is completed before the concessions of travel apply.
